text: The original attention divides the query‑key dot products by \( \sqrt{d_k} \) because without this scaling the dot products can become large in magnitude (especially for large \(d_k\)), pushing the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients. Scaling by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the values in a range where the softmax remains sensitive and gradients are stable[C:attention:9]. The same reasoning is reiterated: dot‑product attention can produce large values, so the scaling counteracts this effect and improves training stability[C:attention:10].

Moshi’s Depth Transformer has **6 layers** and a **model dimension of 1024**[C:moshi:23].

The smoothing module solves the difficulty of training with discrete chunk boundaries – it makes the boundary‑learning operation differentiable so gradients can flow through chunking, prevents unstable or over‑fitted chunk patterns, and provides adaptive error‑correction for low‑confidence chunks[C:dynchunk:22]. It is essential for stable training dynamics, as removing it causes compression‑ratio fluctuations[C:dynchunk:65].

The hierarchical network consists of three stages: (i) a small encoder network that processes the raw data, (ii) a main network that operates on compressed chunks, and (iii) a decoder network that upsamples and processes the data at the original resolution[C:dynchunk:6].

Moshi’s “Inner Monologue” is a modeling technique that first predicts time‑aligned text tokens as a prefix and then generates the corresponding audio tokens from a neural audio‑codec residual quantizer.  By running the text‑to‑speech generation and the user‑speech generation in parallel streams, it removes explicit speaker turns and enables real‑time, full‑duplex spoken dialogue.  The method also allows Moshi to be repurposed as streaming TTS or streaming ASR simply by adjusting the delay between the two token types[C:moshi:1][C:moshi:15].
